query: For high-entropy-alloy bond coats used in thermal barrier coating systems for high-temperature applications, what single intervention could improve coating durability and reliability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying ultrasonic burnishing as a post‐treatment to as‐deposited high‐entropy alloy (HEA) bond coats will refine the near-surface microstructure and induce beneficial compressive residual stresses that reduce oxide spallation during cyclic high‐temperature exposure, thereby improving coating durability and reliability in thermal barrier coating systems.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐deposited HEA bond coat (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA produced by laser cladding) exhibiting a mixed FCC+BCC microstructure with moderate grain sizes and a known tendency for oxide scale spallation under high-temperature (≈900 °C) oxidizing conditions.
generation.intervention: Subject the as‐deposited HEA bond coat to ultrasonic burnishing treatment.
generation.conditions: Cyclic thermal exposure and oxidation tests at temperatures around 900 °C (potentially with molten salt contamination to simulate real service environments) that mimic TBC system operating conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, near-surface microstructure with a gradient of ultra-fine grains and induced compressive residual stresses.
generation.mechanism: Ultrasonic burnishing mechanically deforms the top surface of the coating, refining the grain structure and reducing defect density. The process also introduces compressive residual stresses that are known to retard crack initiation and propagation as well as improve the adhesion of the protective oxide scale formed during high-temperature exposure. This combination is expected to lower the extent of oxide spallation during cyclic thermal and oxidizing environments.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated HEA bond coats, the UB-treated coatings will exhibit a significantly lower oxide spallation area, improved adhesion of the thermally grown oxide (TGO), and enhanced overall durability when subjected to high-temperature cyclic oxidation and thermal shock.
generation.baseline: Untreated as-deposited HEA bond coats that, under identical high-temperature cyclic oxidation conditions, show relatively larger spallation areas (as observed in previous studies with spallation on the order of 5–15%) and grain coarsening that degrades adhesion.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under cyclic temperatures near 900 °C and oxidizing conditions typical of TBC systems; however, its performance under additional challenges (e.g., dual attack by CMAS) remains to be determined.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends findings from studies on ultrasonic burnishing of medium-entropy alloy coatings (e.g., PMC9416578::web::019, where gradient microstructural hardening was achieved) into the HEA bond coat domain, and couples these insights with known issues of oxide scale spallation in HEAs (as discussed in PMC10488378::web::012 and the conflicting spallation data in PMC10488378::web::015). The effectiveness of UB in this specific HEA system and the optimal processing parameters remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of identical HEA bond coat samples by laser cladding. Apply ultrasonic burnishing (using optimized parameters to maximize grain refinement and induce compressive stress) to one group while leaving the other group untreated. Subject both groups to a cyclic oxidation test at ~900 °C (with a molten salt environment if possible) over a set duration that simulates service conditions. Evaluate microstructural evolution, residual stress distribution, and oxide spallation behavior.
measurements: Quantitative spallation area analysis via image processing of post-test surface micrographs
Residual stress measurements using X-ray diffraction
Grain size and microstructural analysis using EBSD
Adhesion strength tests (e.g., pull-off tests) on the oxide scales
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the UB-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxide spallation area, fail to show induced compressive residual stresses compared to controls, or do not demonstrate enhanced oxide adhesion and durability under these cyclic high-temperature conditions, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
